title: Lecture library
text:
Each row is one lecture, grouped by part of the course. The notebooks are from psdv-teaching, which has the source code for the lectures and all rendered notebooks. Recordings of the tutorials are in a YouTube playlist. The Shorts are also collected, in course order, on the Probability and statistics in 1 minute page and in a YouTube playlist.
Slides: chapter slides from Introduction to Probability for Data Science and handwritten notes from class (PDF) · Notebooks: worked code, or a Colab notebook for a lab · Apps: interactive demos · Cheat sheet: a two-page A4 summary (PDF) · Shorts: one-minute videos, each answering one question; point at a number to see the question · Videos: explainers by others (point at one to see its author) · Recording: a tutorial video by the instructor.

title: Lecture library
text:
Random variables and expectation



No.
Lecture
Resources




17 10 Feb
Random variables A random variable is a number worked out from each outcome. Also a discussion of quiz 1.
Slides Cheat sheet Shorts 1 2


18 11 Feb
Probability mass functions The chance of each value, and the common discrete distributions: Bernoulli, binomial, geometric and Poisson.
Slides Notebook Cheat sheet Shorts 1 2 3 4 5 Recording


19 17 Feb
Discrete random variables and expectation The expected value as a long-run average, and the binomial and Poisson distributions.
Slides Expectation, Handwritten notes Notebook Cheat sheet Shorts 1 2 Videos Binomial and Poisson


20 18 Feb
Moments Variance, standard deviation and higher moments, and a first look at continuous random variables.
Slides Moments, Handwritten notes (continued), Continuous variables, handwritten Cheat sheet Shorts 1


21 19 Feb
Lab viva 3 Viva on assignment 3.



22 24 Feb
Continuous random variables and a coin-flip game Densities, where probability is an area, and a coin-flip game that shows how far a total can drift.
Notebooks Expectation, Continuous distributions Cheat sheet Shorts 1 2 3 4


23 25 Feb
Expectation and moments of continuous random variables Mean and variance for a density, by integration. Continues the notebooks of lecture 22.
Slides Handwritten notes Notebooks Expectation, Continuous distributions Cheat sheet Shorts 1


24 17 Mar
Cumulative distribution functions The running total of probability, and how to use it to draw random samples.
Slides Handwritten notes Notebook Cheat sheet Shorts 1 2 3

title: ES 114: Probability, statistics and data visualization
text:
A first-year course on reasoning with uncertainty and data: working with data in Python (NumPy, Pandas and Matplotlib), sets and probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem, random variables and their distributions, expectation and variance, joint distributions, sums of random variables, the law of large numbers, and random vectors and principal component analysis. Every lecture's slides, notebooks, cheat sheet and short videos are in the lecture library.
All communication is on the course Slack: join the ES 114 workspace.

title: ES 114: Probability, statistics and data visualization
text:
Prerequisites
None. This is a first-year undergraduate course.

title: ES 114: Probability, statistics and data visualization
text:
Reference textbooks

Chan, Stanley. "Introduction to Probability for Data Science." The University of Michigan Library, Michigan Publishing (2021). Free digital copy
Adhikari, Ani, John DeNero, and D. Wagner. "Computational and Inferential Thinking: The Foundations of Data Science." Second Edition. The University of California, Berkeley (2019). Free digital copy
Deisenroth, Marc Peter, A. Aldo Faisal, and Cheng Soon Ong. Mathematics for Machine Learning. Cambridge University Press, 2020. Free digital copy
Spiegelhalter, David. The Art of Statistics: Learning from Data. Penguin UK, 2019.
Rougier, Nicolas. Scientific Visualization: Python + Matplotlib. 2021. Free digital copy

title: Uniform Distribution Transformation
text:
import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

%matplotlib inline
%config InlineBackend.figure_format = 'retina'
a, b = 1, 3
num_samples = 100000

uniform_dist = torch.distributions.Uniform(a, b)
X_samples = uniform_dist.sample((num_samples,))

Y_samples = X_samples ** 2

y_values = torch.linspace(a**2, b**2, 500)
f_Y = 1 / (2 * torch.sqrt(y_values) * (b - a))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 6), sharey=True)

axes[0].hist(X_samples.numpy(), bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.6, label="Empirical PDF")
axes[0].axhline(1 / (b - a), color='r', linestyle='--', label="Theoretical PDF")
axes[0].set_xlabel("X ~ Uniform(a, b)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Density")
axes[0].set_title("PDF of Uniform(a, b)")
axes[0].legend()
axes[0].grid()

axes[1].hist(Y_samples.numpy(), bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.6, label="Empirical PDF")
axes[1].plot(y_values.numpy(), f_Y.numpy(), 'r-', label="Theoretical PDF")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Y = X^2")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Density")
axes[1].set_title("Transformation of Uniform(a, b) via Y = X^2")
axes[1].legend()
axes[1].grid()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
\(Y = X^2 \Rightarrow X = \sqrt{Y}\) or \(X = -\sqrt{Y}\)
Since \(X \in [a, b]\) and \(a > 0\), only the positive root is valid.
\[
f_Y(y) = f_X(x(y)) \cdot \left|\frac{dx}{dy}\right| = f_X(\sqrt{y}) \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}
\] And since \(f_X(x) = \frac{1}{b - a}\) (for uniform),
\[
f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{b - a} \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}, \quad \text{for } y \in [a^2, b^2]
\]
\[
f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{2(b - a)\sqrt{y}}, \quad y \in [a^2, b^2]
\]

title: Uniform Distribution Transformation
text:
Exponentional RV
\[
f_X(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \quad x \ge 0
\]
\[
F_X(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}
\]
\[
F_X^{-1}(u) = -\frac{\ln(1 - u)}{\lambda}
\]

lambda_ = 1.0
n_samples = 10000

# Sample from Uniform(0,1)
u = torch.rand(n_samples)

# Apply inverse CDF of exponential
samples = -torch.log(1 - u) / lambda_

# True distribution using torch.distributions
exp_dist = torch.distributions.Exponential(rate=lambda_)

x_vals = torch.linspace(0, 6, 100)
pdf_vals = exp_dist.log_prob(x_vals).exp()  # f_X(x) = λ e^(-λx)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.hist(samples.numpy(), bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.6, label="Inverse CDF Samples")
plt.plot(x_vals.numpy(), pdf_vals.numpy(), 'r-', label="True Exponential PDF")
plt.title("Inverse Transform Sampling using PyTorch")
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("Density")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

title: Frequently asked questions
text:
What are the prerequisites?





The course has no formal prerequisites, like all courses at IITGN. It assumes a basic understanding of programming in Python.









What is the prerequisite exam?





An exam we designed to make sure you have the background needed for the course.









How can I prepare for the prerequisite exam?





Your UG course material should be enough to prepare for it.









What happens if I do not clear the prerequisite exam?





You will not be allowed to take the course.









What does "clear" the exam mean?





As in all courses at IITGN, the instructor decides the cut-off, and you have to score above it. The cut-off is not revealed to students in advance.

title: Frequently asked questions
text:
Laptop policy






Can I use my laptop or phone in class?





No. You may not use your laptop or phone in class for any reason, unless it is a lab session where the instructor has explicitly allowed laptops.

title: Frequently asked questions
text:
Quizzes






What happens if I miss a quiz for any reason?






The quiz is marked 0.
The best 3 of 4 rule is designed with such cases in mind.










Are the quizzes and the end-semester exam open book? Can I bring notes?





No. The exams and quizzes are closed book, and you may not bring notes.









How soon do I get my answer sheets back?





Expect them back in 4 to 5 working days.









Is there a mid-semester or end-semester exam?





2 of the 4 quizzes are held in the mid-semester and end-semester slots. The other two are held during the semester.









Are the quizzes multiple choice or written?





A quiz may have both multiple-choice and written questions.

title: Frequently asked questions
text:
Assignments






What happens if I miss an assignment for any reason?





There are no extensions for assignments.









I have a doubt about an assignment. Whom should I write to?





Ask on the Slack #assignments channel. If you get no response within 2 days, write to the course instructor.









I do not know Python. Can I write the assignments in another language?





No. You have to use Python.









How are assignments evaluated?





Each assignment is followed by a viva. The TAs first check the code against the submission; any change from the submitted code is not allowed, and any instance of it leads to a warning. The TAs then run the code and ask a few questions: about 75% on the assignment itself and about 25% on the theory behind the concepts it covers.

50%


Questions on the assignment and your understanding of the code
25%


Code quality
12.5%


Questions on the theory behind the concepts in the assignment
12.5%












Are assignments individual or in groups?





In groups. All members of a team get the same grade for the assignment.

Attendance is set out in the grading policy.

title: Frequently asked questions

Audit policy






Can I audit the course?





You are free to attend the lectures. However, with a limited number of TAs and a large number of students, we cannot grade your submissions, and you cannot formally contribute to any team's assignments.

Typically we have been kindly given Google Cloud credits. We will update this section once we have them. The credits are more than enough for the assignments.
